summary: A survey of how many hosts accept Telnet connections from a user at a class C site. That requires working IP, TCP, gateway routing via ICMP and handling of class C addresses.

eli5.summary: A check to see how many computers can talk to a small network that uses the newest kind of address.

subtitle: A survey of which hosts on the early Internet could accept Telnet connections from a Class C network.

tldr.problem: It was unclear how many hosts on the Internet could successfully handle Telnet connections from a small network using a newer address class (Class C) that required support for ICMP gateway routing and Class C address handling.
tldr.mechanism: The survey tested Telnet connections from a terminal concentrator on a Class C network (192.1.2.22 at BBN) to hosts listed in RFC 843, recording which ones responded successfully, refused connection, were unreachable, or did not respond.
tldr.outcome: Of 187 hosts tested, 127 (67.9%) accepted Telnet connections. Performance varied by address class: 93.8% on non-Class A networks, 63.6% on Class A network 10, and 58.8% on other Class A networks. This RFC updates RFC 843.

today: RFC 844 is a historic survey that updates RFC 843. It provides a snapshot of Internet host readiness for Class C addressing and ICMP routing in early 1983.

sections.title: Why This Survey Was Done
sections.content:
This survey determined how many Internet hosts could respond to Telnet connections from a user at a Class C network site. The test was important because it required participation in multiple protocol features: IP addressing, TCP (the connection protocol), ICMP gateway routing, and Class C address handling.

The test site was a terminal concentrator located at 192.1.2.22 at BBN, which sat on a Class C network (192.1.2.xxx) connected to the Internet through a routing gateway. This gateway supported ICMP, including redirection and reporting to users.
sections.eli5: They wanted to know: if you are on a small network and want to talk to any computer, how many will talk back? It is important to test all the pieces working together.

sections.title: How the Survey Was Conducted
sections.content:
The host list was extracted from RFC 843, selecting only those hosts listed as accepting Telnet connections. The tests were run manually on 18 February 1983 from 3 PM to 6:30 PM EST, using typed dotted-decimal addresses. Because only three passes were made through the table, a few hosts may have been missed if they were down at those times.

Each host was tested for one of four outcomes: OK (accepted the connection), refused (actively rejected it), no response, or host unreachable. The results were grouped by address class to show how different network categories performed.
sections.eli5: On one day in 1983, someone tried calling 187 computers three times each and wrote down what happened: did it answer, say no, ignore them, or say it was too far away?

sections.title: Results by Network Class
sections.content:
Overall, 127 out of 187 hosts (67.9%) responded successfully. Results varied by address class: hosts on non-Class A networks had the highest success rate at 93.8% (30 out of 32 OK). Hosts on other Class A networks (11.3.x.x, 128.x.x.x, etc.) achieved 58.8% success (20 out of 34 OK). Hosts on the main Class A network 10 had the lowest rate at 63.6% success (77 out of 121 OK).

The detailed results show the name and address of each host tested and its response. This data provides a snapshot of Internet connectivity in early 1983, showing the percentage of hosts that had fully implemented the required protocols for Class C network interoperability.
sections.eli5: Nine out of ten computers on small networks answered back. Six out of ten on the big main network answered. This shows some computers were not yet ready for the new kind of address.

references.text: Harrenstien, K., et al., "Host Table," RFC 843.
